findings.title: Recovery codes held in user storage are never consumed and can be replayed indefinitely
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential pushes the raw generated codes to the user storage via user.credentialManager().updateCredential() and then relies solely on the storage's CredentialInputValidator.isValid() for later verification. Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider (which overwrites the used code's hash on every successful validation), there is no framework hook that marks a code as used in the user storage, and the reference implementation shipped in this PR (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) does a plain anyMatch over the stored codes without consuming anything. Its getCredentials() also rebuilds the credential model from the raw codes, so allCodesUsed() is always false. Consequence: a user whose recovery codes live in user storage can reuse the same code forever, and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is never triggered by code exhaustion - the one-time property of recovery codes is lost for federated users.

findings.title: Raw, unhashed recovery codes are handed to user storage and stored in plaintext by the reference provider
findings.body: Local storage keeps only RS512-hashed recovery codes, but the federated contract introduced here sends the complete list of raw codes inside the UserCredentialModel, and the shipped reference implementation (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential) persists that JSON verbatim as credentialData. Any storage following this pattern keeps recoverable, plaintext recovery codes, unlike the local behavior. Additionally, on the user-storage path the prepared credentialModel (userLabel, generatedAt, hashed codes) is silently discarded, so the storage never receives the label or timestamp. Either the codes should be hashed before being handed over, or the SPI contract must explicitly require storages to hash them and track consumption.

findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById cannot delete a federated recovery-code credential
findings.body: isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid now obtains the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which prefers federated credentials (from getFederatedCredentialsStream(), i.e. owned by the user storage). When allCodesUsed() is true it calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(id), but that method only removes credentials stored in Keycloak's own database - a credential held by a user storage provider (whose id was generated by the provider and is unknown to the local store) is not removed, so the call is a no-op or fails. The exhausted credential stays in the storage, isConfiguredFor() keeps returning true, and the same applies to account-console/admin-REST deletion and disableCredentialType (the reference storage has no recovery-codes handling there either), leaving no removal path for storage-held recovery codes.

findings.title: getCredential prefers federated credentials while validation accepts either store, so the wrong credential can be inspected and stale local codes survive
findings.body: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() returns the federated credential if one exists and only falls back to local storage. However, credentialManager().isValid() accepts a code matching either the user-storage credential or a locally stored credential. If a user has both (for example, recovery codes that were stored locally in Keycloak's DB before the user storage added support for the type, then regenerated into the storage after this change), the authenticator checks allCodesUsed() and performs removal on the federated credential while the user may still be authenticating with the old local credential. The stale local credential is never removed or reported, so previously generated codes remain valid indefinitely alongside the new ones.

findings.title: New recovery-codes user-storage test only covers the happy path and masks the replay bug
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only asserts that codes can be set up in the storage and used once. It does not verify that a used code is rejected on a second login, that exhausting all codes triggers the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action, or that storage-held codes can be deleted/regenerated via the account console or admin REST. These are exactly the behaviors that diverge between local and federated storage - and because the reference BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage never consumes codes and always reports allCodesUsed()==false, a reuse or exhaustion test would currently fail, so the missing assertions hide the replay defect described in the CredentialHelper finding.

findings.title: getCredentials dereferences getMyUser(user) without a null check
findings.body: In getCredentials(RealmModel, UserModel), the result of getMyUser(user) is used directly (myUser.recoveryCodes) even though getMyUser returns null when the user is not present in the map - the null case is explicitly guarded in isConfiguredFor() but not here. A lookup for an unknown user (or a user whose storage id resolves to a missing entry) will throw a NullPointerException from the credential-manager stream instead of returning an empty stream, which can break unrelated credential-listing code paths that call getFederatedCredentialsStream().
